person.name: Giovanni Coutinho
person.title: Platform Engineer
person.intro: I run Kubernetes platforms and build tools for the engineers using them.

bodies.name: Platform engineering
bodies.subtitle: From commit to cluster
bodies.blurb: Multi-cluster EKS, and the delivery path that gets a commit into it without a DevOps engineer standing behind every release.
details: In production platform work I operated multi-cluster Amazon EKS across development, staging, shared services and production. Terraform and Terragrunt described infrastructure, Atlantis ran plans, and Helm and Argo CD delivered services.

I launched and drove a 30+ service migration from GitLab-driven delivery to Argo CD, with kickstart templates and self-service delivery so covered deploys did not need a DevOps engineer at every release.
The moons cover the work that keeps that path usable: running the clusters, delivery, network isolation and incident response.
bodies.lesson: A service owner can ship a reviewed change through the platform.
prompts: How does a change reach a cluster?
What did the GitOps migration involve?
How did you help teams adopt GitOps?

bodies.name: Production operations
bodies.subtitle: Kubernetes day to day
bodies.blurb: I run production Kubernetes. Cluster upgrades, autoscaling, infrastructure as code, and the pager.
details: Multi-cluster EKS, Karpenter node autoscaling, Terraform and Terragrunt, Helm and Atlantis. Capacity planning included requests and limits, reshaping clusters and matching AWS Savings Plans to the fleet.
I ran Aurora/RDS PostgreSQL upgrades against end-of-life deadlines with Blue/Green production cutovers, then turned the upgrade path into an AI skill with a review step before each change.
bodies.lesson: Cluster operations and database upgrades become repeatable workflows.
prompts: What does your Kubernetes work involve?
How do you handle database upgrades?
What infrastructure tools do you use?

bodies.name: Incident response
bodies.subtitle: From the page to the fix that sticks
bodies.blurb: Production on-call for wallet and exchange systems, from the first page through the changes that reduce recurring work.
details: I drove incidents and stakeholder communication in a follow-the-sun team rotation, wrote postmortems, then automated or changed the process to cut toil.
I worked with application teams on SLIs and SLOs, tuned alerts on critical services, and maintained runbooks for the observability stack and cluster upgrades.
bodies.lesson: Restore service, explain the cause, and change the system.
prompts: How do you approach an incident?
Tell me about a hard debugging session.
What happens after service is restored?

bodies.name: Cilium
bodies.subtitle: Isolation as code
bodies.blurb: I drove Cilium onboarding after Calico, then moved the policies into Git so isolation gets reviewed like everything else.
details: It earned itself once. An SSRF probe hit a production fiat path with an attacker-controlled URL. The L7 DNS proxy dropped the callback, IMDS egress was denied, and nothing got a 200 back out. I ran the cluster-wide policy audit afterwards and handed the application sink to the team that owned it.

Getting there meant network-policy CI with Helm templates, and Prometheus exporters so we could see how much of the fleet was actually covered rather than assuming. Then Cilium and the policies moved to GitOps across every environment with ApplicationSets and autoSync. Manual drift reverts itself now.
Later I upgraded Cilium across environments after reading up on DNS-proxy behaviour changes over four minor versions. DNS timeouts measurably improved.
bodies.lesson: Network-policy CI, Helm templates and coverage exporters supported the move to GitOps.
prompts: What did you build around Cilium?
Tell me about the SSRF.
How do network policies fit into GitOps?

bodies.name: Argo CD
bodies.subtitle: Reviewed delivery
bodies.blurb: Argo CD is the delivery path. I onboarded the applications onto it and built the templates that made releases self-serve.
details: I onboarded running applications onto Argo CD and built kickstart templates that made covered releases self-service. Custom migration paths handled services that did not fit a standard chart.
For observability, I reconciled Git with live production exporters and dashboards before turning off the old GitLab deployment paths.
I fixed metric-label provenance so dashboards kept working when services moved from GitLab delivery to GitOps.
bodies.lesson: The migration includes the operational context people depend on.
prompts: What did you contribute to Argo CD adoption?
How did you move observability onto GitOps?
What were the kickstart templates for?

bodies.name: Public tools
bodies.subtitle: Useful things you can inspect
bodies.blurb: Tools built around work I actually do: running a search, handling paper, and exploring model decisions.
details: Each project has public source and a specific job. Open a moon for its purpose, the implementation, and a direct repository link.
The same platform habits show up here: bounded interfaces, observable behavior and a way to inspect what happened.
bodies.lesson: Start with a real task and leave a tool someone else can use.
prompts: Which projects are public?
What does Platen do?
What is Job Scout for?

bodies.name: Job Scout
bodies.subtitle: Running a job search like an operations problem
bodies.blurb: Job Scout is my opportunity desk: the tooling I built to run my own search the way I'd run a platform.
details: A TypeScript monorepo with a Hono API, worker, React UI and PostgreSQL. It discovers listings, applies deterministic gates, and supports triage, research and application materials through a model gateway.
An MCP server lets agent harnesses drive the workflow. The public panel uses an aggregate metrics count; listings, companies and application details stay in the private desk.
bodies.lesson: Discovery, evidence and the next action belong in one workflow.
prompts: What is Job Scout for?
Why build this instead of using a spreadsheet?

bodies.name: Platen
bodies.subtitle: Paper, browsers and agents
bodies.blurb: A printer and scanner server with a web UI, REST API and built-in MCP server.
details: Platen prints PDFs even on printers that only accept raster data, scans from a browser, and files scans in Paperless-ngx.
The published project is a single Go binary that speaks IPP and eSCL directly. The same device is usable by a person, a script or an agent.
bodies.lesson: One device, usable from a browser, script or agent.
prompts: How does Platen support raster-only printers?
How do scanning and Paperless fit together?

bodies.name: Jev Playground
bodies.subtitle: Inspect the model’s decisions
bodies.blurb: Small interactive experiments in typed model decisions, with the request and response visible.
details: The published playground contains twenty local sites built around choice, score and yes/no decisions. Arithmetic, dates and ranking stay in ordinary code.
Each experiment has an x-ray view of its model request and response. Calls happen through an explicit interaction.
bodies.lesson: Make a model’s decision inspectable before building around it.
prompts: What stays in code rather than the model?
What can I inspect in the x-ray view?

bodies.name: Operating homelab
bodies.subtitle: A platform I run at home
bodies.blurb: Talos clusters on Proxmox and bare metal, with GitOps delivery, shared observability and a GPU worker for local models.
details: The lab now separates personal services, business workloads and observability across clusters. Omni manages Talos, Flux reconciles each platform, and Argo CD delivers applications.
The network uses segmented VLANs, Cilium and BGP, with Envoy Gateway at the edge. Cloudflare tunnels carry public traffic and Technitium provides split-horizon DNS.
The live readings aggregate the current cluster fleet. Node labels are anonymized; operational addresses and service inventories stay private.
The moons follow what keeps the lab running: compute, storage, data services, networking, Bitcoin and local models. The public handbook records the reusable operating approach.
bodies.lesson: The lab is where platform choices meet the cost of operating them.
prompts: What runs in the homelab?
How do you handle storage and backups?
Why bare metal?

bodies.name: GPU node
bodies.subtitle: Local images, language and music
bodies.blurb: A bare-metal worker with two RTX 3090s for local image, language and music model experiments.
details: The worker belongs to the personal-services cluster and runs local model tooling, including ComfyUI and Ollama.

Recent work covered real generation jobs, GPU power and thermal behavior, and the trade-offs between model quality and throughput. The hardware lives inside the same operational system of networking, storage and declarative configuration.
bodies.lesson: Measure the actual workload on the hardware that will run it.
prompts: Why run models locally?
What do you use it for?

bodies.name: Bitcoin beacon
bodies.subtitle: My node's mempool
bodies.blurb: Live block height, mempool backlog and fee estimates, read from the node in my own house.
details: A Bitcoin full node supplies chain data; Fulcrum indexes it for Electrum clients, and mempool provides the read-only HTTP interface used here.
The website proxies a small allowlist of mempool endpoints. Node health comes from aggregate exporter metrics. RPC credentials and wallet-query interfaces never reach the browser.
bodies.lesson: A public reading needs only a narrow read-only interface.
prompts: How does Bitcoin fit into your homelab?
Where do these numbers come from?

bodies.name: Network and edge
bodies.subtitle: Deliberate paths in and out
bodies.blurb: Cilium and BGP inside the lab, Envoy Gateway at the edge, and separate paths for public and internal services.
details: Each cluster has its own network segment and load-balancer pool. BGP advertises service addresses to the router; Cilium policies restrict workload traffic.
Public traffic arrives through Cloudflare tunnels. On the LAN, Technitium resolves the same service names to internal gateways.
The previous cluster collected Hubble and Tetragon event streams. Those collectors are not currently reporting from the new fleet, so the panel marks the readings unavailable.
bodies.lesson: Publishing a service is a deliberate routing and policy decision.
prompts: How is the homelab exposed?
What handles DNS?

bodies.name: Storage
bodies.subtitle: Volumes with a physical home
bodies.blurb: Proxmox CSI on ZFS for VM workloads, OpenEBS for bare metal, and NFS for shared storage.
details: VM-backed application volumes use Proxmox CSI. A volume can follow a workload between VMs on the same Proxmox host; it is still tied to that host’s storage.
OpenEBS supplies local storage on the bare-metal worker. NFS covers shared data, and the new clusters use Velero and CloudNativePG backups to object storage on the NAS.
Rook-Ceph and Longhorn are retired. Backup coverage is checked per workload, with volume recovery and database recovery handled separately.
bodies.lesson: Choose placement and recovery together.
prompts: Why Proxmox CSI?
Where does OpenEBS still fit?
How are backups handled?

bodies.name: Data services
bodies.subtitle: PostgreSQL operated with the platform
bodies.blurb: CloudNativePG manages PostgreSQL for application workloads, with database backups alongside volume backups.
details: Database instances are placed with their owning workloads rather than depending on a single shared legacy cluster.
CloudNativePG and its backup integration handle PostgreSQL. A few applications keep their own MariaDB service; the former shared Galera setup is retired.
bodies.lesson: Application placement, database placement and recovery need to agree.
prompts: How do you operate PostgreSQL?
How do database backups differ from volume backups?

bodies.name: Cluster fleet
bodies.subtitle: Virtual machines and bare metal
bodies.blurb: Talos machines managed through Omni, with separate clusters for different workloads.
details: Control planes and general workers run as Proxmox virtual machines; the GPU worker runs on bare metal. Flux installs the platform and Argo CD reconciles applications.
This schematic reads Kubernetes inventory and joins node-exporter readings within each cluster. A missing reading remains unknown, and real node names never reach the page.
bodies.lesson: Inventory and utilization need to refer to the same machine in the same cluster.
prompts: What runs the homelab cluster?
Why Talos instead of a normal distro?

bodies.name: Operator handbook
bodies.subtitle: The reusable part of the lab
bodies.blurb: A public guide to Proxmox, Talos, GitOps and agent-assisted homelab operations.
details: The handbook starts with the network foundation and follows the path through compute, cluster delivery, ingress and agent access.
Its examples describe an operating approach readers can adapt to their own networks. Live readings on this site describe the current lab.
bodies.lesson: Document the operating method so someone else can adapt it.
prompts: Where should a reader start?
How does the handbook connect infrastructure and agents?

bodies.name: Observability
bodies.subtitle: Metrics, logs, traces, and the bill
bodies.blurb: I ran company observability for years and led the move to Grafana Cloud, after making the metrics cheap enough to justify it.
details: I operated company observability across commercial tools, a self-hosted metrics/logs/traces stack, and Grafana Cloud. The path included Prometheus and Thanos, Mimir, Loki, Tempo, and Grafana Alloy.
I led the cardinality program to about 70% reduction by the Grafana Cloud cutover, through keep/drop decisions, instrumentation changes and work with application teams.
After the migration, billable metrics ran at twice the real volume. Mimir HA deduplication across environments fixed the duplicate billing.
The public exporter and this site’s live telemetry show how I keep applying that work.
bodies.lesson: Collect the signals that help people operate the system, and account for their cost.
prompts: Why move to Grafana Cloud?
What did cardinality reduction change?
Tell me about the billing problem.

bodies.name: Site telemetry
bodies.subtitle: The orrery watching itself
bodies.blurb: Everything this site knows about itself, read live from the same Mimir that watches the rest of the homelab.
details: This website exports Prometheus metrics on a private scrape endpoint. Alloy sends them to Mimir; the public API returns selected counts and aggregates.
Flights, questions, opened notes and visited destinations describe browser-reported sessions. They are an estimate of activity, not a verified count of people.
bodies.lesson: The portfolio is an operating service with its own instrumentation.
prompts: Where do these numbers come from?
Why are visitor counts an estimate?
What else do you measure?

bodies.name: Cardinality
bodies.subtitle: Deciding what dies
bodies.blurb: I led the cardinality-reduction program that made the move to Grafana Cloud the cheaper option.
details: It started around 20% off Mimir from scrapers and basic hygiene, and reached about 70% by the cutover. Keep/drop decisions, traces-to-metrics knobs, and a lot of conversations with application teams about how they emit metrics in the first place.
Tooling is good at finding waste. It is not good at deciding what the team can afford to lose, which is the part that took the time.
bodies.lesson: Keep/drop rules, traces-to-metrics settings and application instrumentation drove the reduction.
prompts: How do you reduce cardinality?
What did teams have to change?

bodies.name: Alloy
bodies.subtitle: The ship path, and what it hid
bodies.blurb: Alloy carries the telemetry. It also quietly billed everything twice for a while.
details: The log and metric ship path went Promtail and Fluent first, then Alloy into the on-prem stack, and finally into Grafana Cloud.

After the cutover, billable metrics came in at twice the real volume. Alloy clustering was broken, so the same series shipped twice and got billed twice. Mimir HA deduplication across every environment fixed it.
bodies.lesson: Mimir HA deduplication stopped duplicate series from being billed twice.
prompts: What is Alloy for?
How did you find the double billing?

bodies.name: Dashboards as code
bodies.subtitle: Boards that survive a migration
bodies.blurb: Dashboards provisioned from git, so their real state is the reviewed state.
details: Provisioning boards from files makes them reviewable and stops them drifting in a UI where anyone can nudge a panel and nobody can tell.

The migration to GitOps broke them once. Argo deploys dropped the CI provenance labels the boards grouped on, so panels went blank for migrated services. I made the chart labels source-agnostic and validated it on a pilot service before touching the fleet.
bodies.lesson: Provisioned dashboards and source-agnostic chart labels kept panels working through the GitOps migration.
prompts: Why provision dashboards from git?
What broke during the migration?

bodies.name: Uptime watch
bodies.subtitle: Whether any of it is actually up
bodies.blurb: Uptime Kuma checks configured services and feeds aggregate availability readings into the observability stack.
details: The panel shows the configured monitor count, passing checks, typical thirty-day uptime and soonest certificate expiry. Monitor names, URLs and hostnames stay in the metrics store.
The uptime figure is a median. Passing and failing counts remain visible beside it, and missing metrics stay unavailable.
bodies.lesson: Aggregate uptime needs the passing and failing counts beside it.
prompts: What monitors the homelab?
Why is the uptime a median?

bodies.name: CPA Prometheus
bodies.subtitle: Metrics for a model gateway
bodies.blurb: A Prometheus plugin exposing proxy usage and provider quota through an authenticated management endpoint.
details: The published plugin records traffic, tokens, failures and duration, and polls provider quota windows.
Metrics live behind management authentication. The portfolio links to the source, not to the operational metrics endpoint.
Related public work includes a contribution adding Grok quota display to the CLIProxyAPI management UI.
bodies.lesson: Observe the gateway through the interface it already exposes.
prompts: What does the exporter measure?
How does it integrate with Prometheus?

bodies.name: Agent tooling
bodies.subtitle: Tools engineers actually use
bodies.blurb: MCP servers, shared skills and practical workflows that put engineering tools in the same conversation as the work.
details: In production platform work I authored Observe MCP and Checkly MCP in TypeScript, with tests, versioned releases and setup documentation. Engineers used them for logs, metrics, synthetic checks and alerts.
Alongside the servers, I built a shared skills toolkit and mentored teammates on agent harnesses and reviewable use in production work.
Current public work extends the same interest into local transcription and cross-agent session continuity. Each moon identifies its project and links to published evidence where available.
bodies.lesson: Give engineers useful tools, a repeatable workflow, and the context to use them.
prompts: What tools did you build for platform teams?
How do skills help engineers?
What agent tooling is public?

bodies.name: Observe MCP
bodies.subtitle: Logs and metrics where the work happens
bodies.blurb: I authored Observe MCP to bring logs and metrics into engineering investigations.
details: It became the main path for bringing application logs into an AI session. The DevOps team and engineers on other teams used it.
Building it in-house removed a dependency on a community project that had disappeared and avoided the cost of the vendor alternative.
bodies.lesson: Logs and metrics become tools in the investigation itself.
prompts: What can Observe MCP investigate?
What was your contribution?

bodies.name: Skills toolkit
bodies.subtitle: How DevOps troubleshoots, written down
bodies.blurb: A shared DevOps AI skills and agents toolkit, built so routine platform work stopped queueing on our team.
details: It covers RDS upgrades, platform onboarding, dashboard creation, metric-based investigation and security guardrails, with a shared docs-and-examples repo beside it. Teammates used it day to day, and other teams read it to work out how DevOps troubleshoots production.

I handed the Argo migration skill to the developers instead of running it for them. Same rule when I teach one of these: they share their screen and they type, I talk. I don't take the keyboard to look fast.
bodies.lesson: Developers used the Argo migration skill themselves, with coaching and review.
prompts: What's in the toolkit?
How do you teach this stuff?

bodies.name: Checkly MCP
bodies.subtitle: Synthetics in the same conversation
bodies.blurb: Checkly MCP brings synthetic-monitoring and alerting context into an investigation. I authored it.
details: I authored Checkly MCP in TypeScript to expose synthetic-monitoring and alerting context to agents, with tests, versioned releases and setup documentation.
I hardened it using Trail of Bits methodology and pnpm supply-chain hardening.
bodies.lesson: Synthetic checks put the user-facing symptom next to the investigation.
prompts: What does Checkly MCP add?
Who used it?

bodies.name: Interview Skills
bodies.subtitle: Record, transcribe, learn
bodies.blurb: Public agent skills for local speaker-labelled transcription and organized interview workflows.
details: The transcription workflow processes audio locally after model downloads, producing timestamped transcripts with speaker labels that can be reviewed.
The process skill organizes preparation, round notes and retrospectives. The public repository contains the reusable method and tooling.
bodies.lesson: Keep rehearsal tied to evidence and a specific interview.
prompts: What does an interview preparation session cover?
How are skills organized?

bodies.name: ai-memory contributions
bodies.subtitle: Continuity across agent sessions
bodies.blurb: Upstream contributions to ai-memory, a project for shared memory and handoffs across coding agents.
details: A merged contribution makes a pending handoff visible to Grok after its first tool call, supporting continuation when the harness cannot show it at startup.
The linked pull request is the published contribution. The upstream project supplies the broader memory system.
bodies.lesson: A focused upstream fix can improve every later session.
prompts: What did you contribute to ai-memory?
How does the handoff reach Grok?

bodies.name: BitOps
bodies.subtitle: Kubernetes consultoria
bodies.blurb: My consultancy: Kubernetes operations, GitOps, observability and agent tooling, alongside products built on that platform.
details: BitOps brings platform engineering into teams’ delivery and operational workflows. The company site carries service scope and contact details.
The moons show concrete product work: a browser-based architectural experience, insurance-broker tooling and scheduling software in testing.
bodies.lesson: Services, product work and contact details live on the BitOps site.
prompts: What does BitOps focus on?
Where can I learn more?

bodies.name: Plano Adentro
bodies.subtitle: Architectural projects in the browser
bodies.blurb: A live pilot where architects and interior designers share projects their clients can explore.
details: A Three.js plan view and walkable interior make the project available in the browser.
Isolated Blender and SketchUp conversion jobs run on Kubernetes, with WhatsApp-code sign-in, expiring share links and scoped OAuth MCP tools.
bodies.lesson: Architectural projects in the browser
prompts: What does Plano Adentro do?
How does Plano Adentro work?

bodies.name: Seguros MCP
bodies.subtitle: Insurance operations for agents
bodies.blurb: MCP tooling for Brazilian insurance-broker workflows over a partner portal.
details: Authenticated sessions support policy and installment reads, searches, claims and documents through tool profiles for agent harnesses.
The consultancy site is the public point of contact for this work.
bodies.lesson: Insurance operations for agents
prompts: What does Seguros MCP do?
How does Seguros MCP work?

bodies.name: Navalha
bodies.subtitle: Scheduling · in testing
bodies.blurb: Scheduling software for barber shops and other appointment-based businesses, with WhatsApp and AI integration.
details: The project is in testing and not yet released. It explores the scheduling workflow for appointment-based businesses.
bodies.lesson: Scheduling · in testing
prompts: What does Navalha do?
How does Navalha work?

bodies.name: Resume station
bodies.subtitle: Giovanni Coutinho
bodies.blurb: I'm Gio. Platform engineer in Belo Horizonte, working remote. I started in Linux and enterprise networks and ended up running Kubernetes platforms and building the tooling around them.
details: 17+ years in IT and 8+ years operating production Kubernetes. For almost seven years at Exodus Movement I designed, shipped and operated multi-cluster AWS/EKS platforms for a non-custodial crypto wallet and exchange.
The thread is making the platform usable by other engineers: self-service GitOps, shared troubleshooting tools, and production MCP servers with the skills and mentoring to use them.
Before Exodus, I worked on Kubernetes delivery for client teams and on enterprise networking, Linux, virtualization and monitoring. The full career record, education and languages are in the resume.
bodies.lesson: Start with the platform work, explore the tools, or read the full resume.
prompts: What kind of platform work do you do?
How do you use AI in engineering?
What did you do before Kubernetes?

bodies.name: Survey array
bodies.subtitle: The whole orrery
bodies.blurb: The whole system from one vantage. Every planet with its moons, and a course you can set without flying there first.
details: Wandering is fine, and slow. When you actually want something, come up here, pick it off the chart, and let Nómada fly it.
bodies.lesson: Pick a destination and the ship takes the course.
prompts: How do I fly to a moon?
Where can I read the resume?

bodies.name: Heliograph
bodies.subtitle: A quiet flash
bodies.blurb: A small relay on the sunward side. If you want me to know you came through, this is how. Name and note are optional.
details: Nothing here is about my work. It's just a way to say hello. A ping carries where you were in the orrery and a little about your connection, and the transport it rides on stays off the site.
bodies.lesson: Get close, then transmit.
prompts: What is this relay?
Does a ping require a name?

bodies.name: Umbra
bodies.subtitle: No sun here
bodies.blurb: A relay in the star's shadow. Hard to spot until you're nearly on top of it.
details: Line up near heading 180 when you ping and the log will say so. The rest is between you and the dark side.
bodies.lesson: Look at the star, then look behind it.
prompts: Why is this so close to the star?

bodies.name: Ghost frequency
bodies.subtitle: Silent until you listen
bodies.blurb: A frequency out on the rim. It stays quiet until you've done the reading.
details: Collect signal buoys around the system. The rim answers after four of them.
bodies.lesson: Fragments first. Then the rim.
prompts: How do I hear this frequency?
